The Marbled frogmouth (Podargus ocellatus) exhibits several key life-history traits that have been characterized through field studies and captive observations. Hatchlings emerge from eggs incubated at a steady temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C] after a developmental period of approximately 30 days [ab = approximately 30 days]. The initial wet weight of a newly hatched chick is remarkably low at 13.5 grams [Ww0 = 13.5 grams], reflecting the altricial state of these nestlings, which are entirely dependent on biparental provisioning. This modest body mass at hatching is typical of caprimulgiform birds, which invest heavily in a relatively small number of offspring. The subsequent growth trajectory is rapid, fueled by a diet of insects and other small invertebrates delivered by both parents throughout the nestling phase.

As the nestling develops, it undergoes a predictable sequence of physiological milestones under the thermal conditions typical of an active adult bird's body temperature, measured at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. Fledging, the point at which the young bird achieves its first sustained flight and leaves the nest, occurs at 30 days after hatching [tx = 30 days after hatching] at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This marks a critical transition from a stationary, nest-bound existence to a mobile, though still dependent, juvenile stage. Sexual maturity, or the attainment of puberty, is reached considerably later, at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching], a delay that allows for the completion of skeletal growth and the development of the flight musculature necessary for a predatory lifestyle at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. These developmental timings are critical for understanding the species' reproductive scheduling in its subtropical rainforest habitat.

The species is distinctly sexually dimorphic in terms of adult body mass. Field measurements indicate that adult females achieve a maximum body mass of 170 grams [Wwi = 170 grams], while their male counterparts are substantially larger, reaching an ultimate wet weight of 262 grams [Wwi = 262 grams]. This reversed sexual size dimorphism, where females are slightly smaller than males, is unusual among birds but has been documented in other frogmouth species and is thought to relate to differences in foraging roles or territorial defense. The energetic cost of maintaining this large body size is reflected in the basal metabolic rate. Respirometry trials conducted on resting individuals at a body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C] recorded a maximum oxygen consumption of 102 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 102 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value consistent with the low metabolic rates characteristic of sit-and-wait predators.

Reproductive output in the Marbled frogmouth is characterized by a slow pace of life. Females produce a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], typically laying 1 to 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 1 to 2 eggs per clutch]. The age at which a female first successfully breeds is not until 730 days after hatching [tR = 730 days after hatching], a protracted delay that contrasts with many other bird species of comparable size at a temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]. This deferred first reproduction is likely a consequence of the time required to secure a suitable territory and develop the foraging proficiency needed to sustain a breeding attempt. Under the thermal conditions of the active adult (38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C]), this reproductive strategy aligns with a long-term investment in offspring survival over a high annual fecundity, a pattern typical of tropical and subtropical forest birds.

The overall lifespan of the Marbled frogmouth further underscores its slow life-history strategy. The oldest documented individuals have been recorded to live for approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years] under field conditions at an average active body temperature of 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], a longevity that is remarkable for a bird of its body mass. This extended lifespan is complemented by low annual adult mortality, likely due to its cryptic plumage and nocturnal, sedentary habits that minimize predation risk. The combination of a low reproductive rate, delayed maturity, and long lifespan positions Podargus ocellatus as a classic K-selected species, well adapted to the relatively stable but resource-limited environment of the eastern Australian rainforests where it is endemic. Ongoing research continues to refine these demographic parameters.
